items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: We went to Europe with a group that included Zoot Sims and Roy Eldridge and Toots Thielemans joined us.

ctx.x: He’d already had his whole swing thing.

Yeah. We went to Europe with a group that included Zoot Sims and Roy Eldridge and Toots Thielemans joined us. He wasn’t yet an American, he was still living in Belgium. Charlie Short, the English bass player, the singer Nancy Reed, who am I leaving out? That’s about it. It was a wonderful thing. Some of those performances were recorded, too, I have tapes of some of them that were recorded for a radio program in Sweden and one or two others I guess that were somewhere else on the tour. We played Sweden and…
Did you notice a difference in playing over there? Because a number of people have talked about the difference in the way the music is accepted, or the artists, between the United States and Europe.

items.title: Toots Thielemans — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I learned a lot harmonically from Dick Hyman. He was already, he had already played on the Street... And I learned a lot from him.

ctx.x: So how did that come about?

That was with Roy Eldridge and Zoot Sims and Dick Hyman, a good pianist. And Ed Shaughnessy, the drummer who played a lot for the Johnny Carson Show. And an English bass player, Charlie [Short?]. And I played and Benny Goodman was in love with that Stardust, too, because that’s when he heard. And we have a recording of that Stardust in the [Lausanne?], when we played with Benny Goodman in Europe. And no… we were playing… I could play it for you on my iPad or uPad or [inaudible]. [laughs]
Maybe after we take a break, we can set it up. Sure.
